title: Given final int a = 20, can you assign it to another variable, and what are the rules?
shortTitle: Given final int a = 20, can you assign it to another variable, and the rules

s1_definition.profdef: Yes. A `final` variable can be freely read and its value copied into any number of other variables; `final` only forbids reassigning the final variable itself, not using its value. When you write `int b = a`, you read the value 20 from the final variable `a` and copy it into `b`, which is a normal read operation that `final` never restricts. The rule is that a final variable must be assigned exactly once and then can never be reassigned, but reading it and copying its value is always allowed.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine `final int a = 20` is like a permanently fixed interest rate of 20 printed on an official rate card. Rajesh cannot erase and rewrite the number on that official card, because it is final. But he can absolutely read the 20 off the card and copy it onto his own worksheet, his customer's quote, and a report, as many times as he likes. Copying the value out is always fine; only changing the original card is forbidden.
s1_definition.oneliner: A final variable can be read and copied anywhere; final only blocks reassigning the final variable itself.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Yes. A `final` variable can be freely read and its value copied into any number of other variables; `final` only forbids reassigning the final variable itself, not using its value. When you write `int b = a`, you read the value 20 from the final variable `a` and copy it into `b`, which is a normal read operation that `final` never restricts. The rule is that a final variable must be assigned exactly once and then can never be reassigned, but reading it and copying its value is always allowed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine `final int a = 20` is like a permanently fixed interest rate of 20 printed on an official rate card. Rajesh cannot erase and rewrite the number on that official card, because it is final. But he can absolutely read the 20 off the card and copy it onto his own worksheet, his customer's quote, and a report, as many times as he likes. Copying the value out is always fine; only changing the original card is forbidden.

**One line to remember:** A final variable can be read and copied anywhere; final only blocks reassigning the final variable itself.

sections.s2_technical:
When you declare `final int a = 20`, the variable `a` is permanently bound to the value 20. The `final` modifier prevents any later statement like `a = 30`, which would be a compile error. But it places no restriction on reading `a`.

Assigning to another variable, such as `int b = a`, is a read followed by a write to `b`. The read of `a` yields 20, and that value is copied into `b`. The variable `b` is completely independent. If `b` is not final, you can later change `b` freely, and this does not affect `a` at all, because for primitives the value is copied, not shared.

You can also copy `a` into another final variable, as in `final int c = a`. That is allowed because `c` is being assigned for the first and only time. What you cannot do is reassign `a` itself after its initialization.

A senior nuance appears with compile-time constants. Because `a` is a `final` primitive initialized with a constant expression, the compiler treats `a` as a true compile-time constant and performs constant folding: everywhere `a` is used, the compiler can substitute the literal 20 directly into the bytecode. This is why `final` primitive constants can be used in contexts that require compile-time constants, such as `case` labels in a switch and array sizes. A second nuance is the difference between primitives and references. For `final int a = 20`, copying copies the value. But for a `final` reference like `final Account acc = ...`, copying copies the reference, so `Account other = acc` makes `other` point at the same object; `final` still only stops reassigning `acc`, and both references can still mutate the shared object if it is mutable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank fixes a promotional bonus rate as a final constant so it cannot be tampered with mid-run. The interest engine still needs to read that rate and copy it into per-account calculations. This is exactly the rule that a final variable can be read and copied freely, just not reassigned.

Problem 2 — A developer tried to adjust the final rate inside a loop and got a compile error, then correctly copied it into a local working variable to adjust per customer. This is exactly the distinction between reassigning the final itself versus copying its value into a mutable variable.

Problem 3 — The team wants to use the final rate as a compile-time constant in a switch that classifies tiers. This is exactly what constant folding of a final primitive enables.

The code has a `RateCard` holding a final rate, an `InterestEngine` that copies the final rate into working variables and uses it in a switch, and a `FinalAssignDemo` main class.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a final int a equal to 20, and Rajesh's principal of 1,000,000 rupees.

Step 1: The final variable a is initialized to 20. This binding is now permanent and cannot be reassigned.

Step 2: The statement int b = a reads the value 20 from a and copies it into b. This is a legal read of a final variable. b is independent and not final.

Step 3: The statement final int c = a copies 20 into c. This is legal because c is assigned exactly once, even though it is final.

Step 4: b is changed to b plus 5, giving 25. This is allowed because b is not final, and it has no effect on a, which is still 20, proving the copy was by value.

Step 5: The rate 20 is passed into classifyTier. Because the literal 20 matches the case label, the account is classified into the PROMO tier. This works because the final primitive acts as a compile-time constant.

Step 6: The rate 20 is used to compute monthly interest on the principal using BigDecimal, and the result is logged. Throughout, a was read many times but never reassigned.

```text
INFO: a (final) = 20
INFO: b (copied then +5) = 25
INFO: c (final copy of a) = 20
INFO: Rate 20% classified as PROMO tier
INFO: Interest for SAV2001 (Rajesh) = Rs.16666.67
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  final int a = 20   (locked binding)
    │ read value 20
    ├────────────→ int b = 20   (independent, NOT final)
    │                  │ b = b + 5
    │                  ▼ b = 25   (a unaffected)
    ├────────────→ final int c = 20  (assigned once, OK)
    │
    └────────────→ classifyTier(20) → switch case 20 → PROMO tier
                   monthlyInterest(1000000, 20) → Rs.16666.67

  Forbidden path: a = 30  ✗  (compile error: reassign final)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — final Read vs Reassign ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │        InterestEngine         │
  │ ─────────────────────────────│
  │ + classifyTier(final int):void│  param read-only; used as switch label

  │     BigDecimal, int):BigDecimal│

  Rules for final variables:
    READ  (int b = a)          → ALLOWED (copy value)
    COPY to final (final c = a)→ ALLOWED (c assigned once)
    USE in switch case label   → ALLOWED (compile-time constant folding)
    REASSIGN (a = 30)          → COMPILE ERROR

  Primitive vs reference:
    final int        → copy copies the VALUE (b independent)
    final Object ref → copy copies the REFERENCE (shared object)
                       final still only blocks rebinding the ref
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, given final int a equals 20, I can absolutely assign it to another variable. The key point is that the final keyword only forbids reassigning the final variable itself; it never restricts reading its value or copying that value elsewhere.

When I write int b equals a, that is a read of a, which yields 20, followed by a write into b. The variable b is completely independent, and because this is a primitive the value is copied, not shared, so if I later change b to 25 it has no effect on a, which remains 20. I can even copy a into another final variable, like final int c equals a, because c is being assigned for the first and only time. The one thing I cannot do is write a equals 30 after initialization, because that reassigns the final variable, which is a compile error.

There is a nice senior-level detail here. Because a is a final primitive initialized with a constant expression, the compiler treats it as a true compile-time constant and does constant folding, substituting the literal 20 wherever a is used. That is why such a final constant can be used in places that demand a compile-time constant, like a switch case label or an array size.

I also keep in mind the difference between primitives and references. For a final primitive, copying copies the value. But for a final reference, copying copies the reference, so another variable ends up pointing at the same object, and final still only prevents rebinding the reference, not mutating a shared mutable object. In our banking rate engine this is exactly how it plays out: the promotional rate is a final constant that every worker reads and copies into its own working variable for per-account calculations, but no worker can ever reassign the shared rate, which keeps the promotion consistent and tamper-proof across the whole run.
